items.body:
## What this is

Drew, 2026-10-29: find where OpenCode-native scheduled tasks can replace the Muse cron jobs that currently launch OpenCode — to save Muse tokens or raise throughput — with proper management and monitoring of those tasks and their outcomes. Study: ~/workspace/research_notes/opencode-scheduled-tasks-20261029/findings.md.

## Verdict: PARTIAL — the trigger exists, in OpenChamber, not OpenCode

- **OpenCode core has no scheduler.** Zero cron/timer code in packages/core|server|cli; sessions are purely event-driven.
- **OpenChamber has a real scheduled-tasks subsystem** (packages/web/server/lib/scheduled-tasks/): cron/daily/weekly/once with timezones, per-project + chats scopes, new-session-per-run (model/agent pinning, permission auto-accept, goal mode with token budget, sessions stamped metadata.kind='scheduled') or prompt-into-existing-session, cross-instance occurrence claiming, loop files (.agents/loops/*.md), REST + UI + CLI + an agent tool (openchamber_schedule).
- But it is a **prompt scheduler, not a job system**: state holds only the last run, no token capture, no alerting, in-code defaults of 4 global / 2 per-project concurrent runs, and a 30-minute run cap (vs ~90-minute shift windows).

## Migration waves (Claude input tokens, trailing-24h, runtime-DB attribution)

**Wave 1 (~3.4B/day of the fleet's ~5.1B/day):**
1. **Repo-queue worker shifts — ~2.26B/day, save ~2.1–2.2B.** The Muse layer is claim/checkpoint/terminal-verbs via repo-queue.py plus implementation over laptop-ssh — the identical runbook an OpenCode session already executes when dispatcher-launched. Ports near-verbatim as per-queue scheduled tasks. Blockers: repo-queue.py must run laptop-side; sandbox lane-lock files replaced by the atomic DB claim; run cap raised.
2. **Issue creators — ~0.96B/day, save ~0.9B.** The runbook already is a self-contained prompt. One API-created scheduled task per repo-lane. Note: this reprices the 3.93M-Claude-tokens/filed-issue figure behind Drew's held creator-throttle decision into pool tokens.
3. **OpenChamber dispatcher + babysitter — ~390M/day, save ~350–370M.** The most rule-bound jobs in the fleet, currently spending Claude tokens operating the API of the system that would run the loop natively. Port as existing-session scheduled pokes into persistent sessions (cross-round state lives in session context instead of being re-read at ~1.4M/run).

**Wave 2 (~0.25B):** fleet-monitor, pr-diff pair, issue-sweep, pool-quota-steward (partial fits).

**Keep on Muse:** fleet-watchdog (it is the monitor — it must instead gain coverage of the OpenChamber tasks) and orchestration-pass (the consumer/escalation collector).

## The honest trade

The throughput ceiling moves from Claude-subscription/cron concurrency to **pool quotas + the laptop's 12-session cap**. At a known-100% pool the native fleet stalls where Muse lanes currently sail past. This makes the migration dependent on the full-quota utilization program (#2173) keeping pools fed and rotated.

## Gating monitoring gaps (fix before migrating anything)

1. **Per-run history** — scheduled-task state is last-run-only (laptop JSON). Consume the already-emitted `openchamber:scheduled-task-ran` SSE events into Supabase.
2. **Token accounting** — every OpenCode assistant message already carries cost + tokens (schema/session-message.ts), but nothing exports it; the mirror covers only the Muse runtime. Build an OpenCode-side exporter twin of runtime-db-export (this is #2072 work).
3. **Failure alerting / dead-man's switch** — fleet-watchdog polls GET /api/openchamber/scheduled-tasks/status + queue-claim staleness.
4. **Server residency** — the scheduler dies with the OpenChamber server process; confirm the laptop deployment is always-on (not socket-activated or idle-stopped).
5. **Shared-state locality** — fleet bookkeeping (backlogs, sweep.log, lane locks) is sandbox-resident; OpenCode sessions are laptop-resident. Move per-job state to Supabase, following the queue pattern.
6. Identity binding (task id / session id / queue task id in one place), the loop-file approval gate (silently pauses migrated jobs), escalation path for urgent classes.

## Acceptance

- Gaps 1–4 closed and demonstrated on one pilot: ONE queue lane running as an OpenChamber scheduled task for 48h with per-run history, token accounting, and watchdog coverage — reviewed against its Muse-cron baseline (outcome, tokens, time), then a go/no-go for the rest of wave 1.

## Acceptance criteria

- Each Muse cron wrapper that launches OpenCode is inventoried (in the linked study or a comment here) with a disposition: migrated to an OpenChamber scheduled task, kept on Muse cron with a named reason, or retired.
- Migrated tasks run in waves with monitoring gates between waves: a wave's runs are observed completing (run records + outcome checks) before the next wave migrates.
- For every migrated task, the Muse-token cost change is measured or explicitly estimated, and any throughput change is noted — the migration's stated purpose is token savings or throughput, so the result must say which it got.

# Session dispatch + babysitting (OpenChamber program)

## Purpose
Move the fleet's larger code work off Claude cron shifts — whose every turn re-buys a large context — onto OpenChamber-hosted OpenCode sessions running on plan pools, watched by ONE babysitter worker instead of one worker per issue. Design record: `openchamber-dispatch-babysitter-design-2026-10-26.md` (keep-the-four-repos-healthy goal workspace, files/).

## Scope
- **Locations abstraction:** a session executor is a location (kind: openchamber | opencode-server | openclaw | codex-aster) with an adapter + capacity, so more OpenChamber machines, an OpenClaw gateway, or a Codex `.aster` route plug in without changing the babysitter loop. First location: the laptop's OpenChamber.
- **Dispatcher with admission control:** hands queue tasks marked `executor: openchamber` to sessions only when a slot is free and the routed pool passes the quota measurement gate; otherwise hands the task back (parked `executor-saturated`, noted on the issue) — never a silent backlog.
- **One babysitter:** rounds over every bound session — progress verdicts, one stall nudge then escalation, quota walls as named parks, harvesting finished sessions into verified terminal queue states. Reports quota per pool and a routing ledger (pool used per session, escalations, burn per landed task).
- **Routing, Workhorse-first:** Fast / Workhorse (default) / Frontier tiers per the POOL MAP; Frontier only on evidence or for the design half of a split (Frontier plans, Workhorse/Fast implements).
- **OpenClaw long-term path:** babysitting-by-comment — the monitor's routine issue comment is the control channel; OpenClaw reports and obeys in-thread. Reached via pilot → mirror mode → handover (see the design record).

## Execution mode
Online. Builds land as fleet job bodies, helper tooling, and Supabase/queue conventions under the fleet goal; session work happens on the laptop location.

## Dependencies
- Babysitter v1 (#1185) depends on the session-API inventory pilot (#1188).
- Dispatch v1.1 (#1187) is blocked by #1185, #1188, and the quota-attribution pilot (#1189).
- Routing thresholds wait on the routing pilot (#1191); stall detection waits on the stall-taxonomy pilot (#1192); OpenClaw mirror mode waits on the comment-loop pilot (#1190).

## Acceptance
- The babysitter runs as one worker regardless of session count; every dispatched task ends in a verified terminal state or a named hand-back.
- A week of babysitter reports shows per pool: sessions run, landed rate, Frontier escalations with reasons, quota burn per landed task.
- OpenClaw comment-loop pilot produces a go/no-go for mirror mode with the comment format pinned if go.

Filed by Muse (operator) 2026-10-26 under Drew's direction (design + issues filed the same evening; this epic groups them for the roadmap and PM dashboard).

## What this is

Drew, 2026-10-29: the fleet's job execution runs on effectively one machine (the laptop, amd-6 — OpenCode server, queue workers, OpenClaw gateway). He wants (1) additional machines set up so they can be used for jobs the same way the laptop is used now, and (2) the fleet structure redesigned to connect to a **pool of machines** instead of a single host.

## Work

1. **Machine onboarding standard.** Define what a machine needs to join the pool: NixOS config from the flake, SSH access pattern, OpenCode server (attach pattern), queue worker capability, health reporting, and the secrets it may hold (by name only). A machine joins by applying the standard, not by hand-crafting.
2. **Bring the additional machines online.** The hardware exists (the Threadripper fleet in the basement, Osseo WI) — the on-site evidence cluster (code#1095/#1097/#1099/#1101) is the inventory input and is Drew's physical step. As machines are inventoried and installed, onboard them one by one against the standard. Relationship to the lab-cluster goal (Talos/Cozystack): that program stands up the Kubernetes cluster; THIS issue is about machines as fleet job-execution nodes. Where a machine serves both, the standard says so explicitly — do not let the two programs silently diverge.
3. **Redesign the fleet structure for a pool.** Today: hardcoded laptop assumptions (the 12-session cap, SSH target, scheduler residency, watchdog locality). Target: a machine registry (identity, capabilities, capacity, health), placement that picks a machine per job/session (the route-pool idea, one level down: machine pools beside model pools), and schedulers (Muse cron, OpenChamber scheduled tasks #2174, OpenClaw automations #2177) placing work across the pool. Observability follows the same move: per-machine attribution joins the per-job/per-model attribution in #2072 and the Supabase mirror.
4. **Failure shape.** A machine leaving the pool (off, overloaded, network) drains cleanly: its sessions/jobs are visible as orphaned in one place, and no other machine's state is corrupted (the plaza-objects/shared-state lessons).

## Acceptance

- The onboarding standard written and applied to the first additional machine end-to-end: it runs a real queue job and an OpenCode session, reviewed like laptop work.
- The registry exists and the watchdog covers every pooled machine.
- A written placement design (which scheduler places what, on which signals) with the first placement rule live.

## Related

Hardware evidence cluster code#1095/#1097/#1099/#1101 (Drew, on-site) · lab-cluster goal · #2072 observability · #2174 OpenChamber scheduled tasks · #2177 OpenClaw scheduled tasks · #2173 quota utilization (pool quotas are the other half of the throughput ceiling).

items.body:
## Purpose

Drew (2026-10-27, with the Muse usage upgrade): the fleet has token
headroom now — spend it on throughput and on intelligence about the
fleet's own routing. This epic scales the lane pattern to every queue
and every producer, puts the OpenChamber dispatcher and babysitter
live, and builds the oversight stack that keeps the model pools
honest: a quota/config steward that makes bounded routing decisions
and logs every change, a meta-reviewer that grades the reviewers
and updates their guidelines, and a pool-intelligence function that
combines Artificial Analysis data with our own measured session
speeds to flag models to add or retire, with controlled tests.

## Scope (children)

- Lane scale-out: A/B shifts for the opencode, openchamber, and nix
  queues (implements #1130's pattern for all queues).
- Producer lanes: second offset lanes for the issue creator and the
  PR diff reviewer.
- Dispatcher v1 live (extends #1187): launches OpenCode/OpenChamber
  sessions for queued issues under admission control.
- Babysitter live (extends #1185): rounds over ALL OpenCode sessions
  on an interval, with verdicts, quota, and pool attribution.
- Quota & config steward: monitors every pool's quota, makes bounded
  ad-hoc routing decisions (config changes land ONLY via PR to the
  canonical repo config), and keeps an append-only change-event
  ledger with before/after quota snapshots and measured impact.
- Meta-reviewer: reviews the reviewers' (steward, lanes, dispatcher,
  babysitter) activity and outcomes; updates the reviewer guidelines
  from evidence — when model-up/effort-down wins, when max effort is
  waste, which pools earn their place.
- Pool intelligence: Artificial Analysis monitoring + our own
  measured session speed per provider/model/effort; an interpretive
  model combining AA scores with our history; add/retire flags with
  quantified tradeoffs (score vs speed vs cost per pool), validated
  by controlled tests before a change is recommended.

## Execution mode

Scheduled fleet (cron lanes + steward/reviewer/intelligence jobs
under the keep-the-four-repos-healthy goal), reporting to the token /
fleet side chat. Config authority stays canonical: repo PRs only,
never hand-edited deployed files. Credentials by name only.

## Dependencies

- #1234 (OpenChamber dispatch + babysitter design/pilots) — this
  epic operationalizes it.
- #1271 (paired-client enrollment) gates remote babysitter/
  dispatcher reach; early runs measure around it from the laptop.
- #1272 (routing-policy alignment) feeds the steward's decision
  bounds; the steward starts conservative until it lands.

## Acceptance criteria

- [x] All children filed, labelled, and linked as sub-issues.
- [ ] Every job named in the children exists as a live cron with a
      written instruction file, verified by cron list/status.
- [ ] The change-event ledger exists and every config change in the
      window has a matching event with before/after quota snapshots.
- [x] Roadmap rows added for this epic (child issue tracks it).

Filed by Muse (operator) 2026-10-27 on Drew's direction.

items.body:
## What

v1.1 of the OpenChamber dispatch system (design:
`files/openchamber-dispatch-babysitter-design-2026-10-26.md`): turn
the report-only babysitter into the working dispatcher + babysitter.

## Scope

- **Dispatcher:** claims queue tasks whose packet carries
  `executor: openchamber` (larger code work: effort/m+l, session-shaped
  per triage), admits against (a) location capacity and (b) the POOL
  MAP measurement gate for the routed pool (fresh quota read; ≥85% of
  window = no new heavy work). Creates the session in a per-task
  worktree on branch `queue/<task-id>-<issue>-<slug>` and records the
  binding (session id, location, pool/route, started-at) on the task.
- **Hand-back:** no slot or no headroom → park the task with reason
  class `executor-saturated` and note it on the issue. Saturation is
  reported, never a silent backlog; a Claude lane can still claim the
  task if urgent.
- **Babysitter actions:** stall nudge (one message into a session idle
  >20 min while claiming work: checkpoint/continue/state blocker; max
  2, then escalate to the monitor tracker); wall handling (quota stop =
  park blocked with the wall named, never a PAYG fallback); harvesting
  (session done → verify against GitHub → complete/park/block the task
  with labels synced and an agent-note on the issue).
- **Routing policy as config:** Fast / Workhorse (default) / Frontier
  tiers per the design; escalation to Frontier requires recorded
  evidence (failed Workhorse attempt or design-shaped triage); the
  split pattern (Frontier plan → Workhorse/Fast implementation) is a
  first-class dispatch shape. Routing ledger entries land in the
  babysitter report.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] A task marked `executor: openchamber` flows queue → session →
      PR → verified terminal queue state with no Claude lane involved.
- [ ] With the location at capacity, the next candidate is handed back
      (parked, `executor-saturated`, issue noted) within one round.
- [ ] A deliberately stalled session receives exactly one nudge, and a
      second stall escalates instead of nudging forever.
- [ ] Every Frontier session in a week of reports has a recorded
      escalation reason; Workhorse-first is the observed default.
- [ ] No dispatched task evaporates: every binding ends in a terminal
      state or a named hand-back (monitor Duty 1 stays clean).

Depends on: babysitter v1 (report-only) and the session-API + quota
attribution pilots. Filed by Muse (operator) 2026-10-26.

items.body:
## What this is

Drew, 2026-10-29: find where OpenClaw's own scheduled tasks can replace Muse tasks, with management and monitoring of those tasks and outcomes. Study + live smoke test: ~/workspace/research_notes/openclaw-scheduled-tasks-20261029/findings.md. Companion to #2171 (setup + job passing + the OpenCode comparison review).

## Verdict: the scheduler is fleet-grade and idle

- Gateway live and healthy (user service since 2026-10-28 20:43 CDT, HTTP 200, OpenClaw 2026.10.7).
- `openclaw automations` (alias `cron`) is a full scheduler: cron/every/at/on-exit/stream schedules; agentTurn / command / script payloads; isolated or bound sessions; per-job model, fallbacks, thinking level; announce/webhook/no-deliver delivery; failure alerts after 2 consecutive failures; backoff, catch-up runs, restart reconciliation.
- Ledgers live in ~/.openclaw/state/openclaw.sqlite (cron_jobs, cron_run_receipts, task_runs) — status, duration, error, summary. **No token columns**: token review must join each run's session transcript/agentMeta, and OpenClaw usage never enters the runtime DB — migrated jobs leave the Supabase export's attribution unless the ledgers get bridged (that bridge is #2072 work).
- Today exactly two managed jobs exist (hourly heartbeat-main; Memory Dreaming Promotion). No fleet work has ever been scheduled through it. The heartbeat currently SKIPS hourly (`heartbeat skipped: no-route` — no channel binding for main) and inbound webhooks are disabled (POST /hooks/agent → 404).

## Smoke test (2026-10-29, first job ever passed — review row #1)

- Route: `openclaw agent --agent main --session-key smoke-20261029 --json`. One real blocker found and cleared: a bare SSH shell cannot resolve the gateway token SecretRef; the documented fix is exporting OPENCLAW_GATEWAY_TOKEN from ~/.secrets/openclaw/gateway-token (value through process env only).
- Result packet: outcome ok (runId a323dfd6…), **13,746 input / 237 output tokens, $0 recorded, 11.8s gateway time** (74s wall including CLI startup at laptop load ~20). Answer quality good with one honest gap (described fleet peers from workspace docs instead of enumerating the actual second gateway agent, `opencode`).
- **KEY CATCH: the agent's configured primary — commandcode/deepseek/deepseek-v4-flash — failed 401** (the still-pending Command Code sign-in) and the run succeeded only by falling back to design-code/deepseek-v4.1-flash. Gate: fix the Command Code sign-in or repoint the primary before relying on OpenClaw runs.
- Cost shape for the review: a watchdog-class periodic digest costs ~376K Claude input tokens per run on Muse; an equivalent OpenClaw isolated run costs ~14K pool tokens and **zero** Muse subscription tokens (different budget, not free — pool quota).

## Migration candidates

1. **Watchdog-class periodic digests** (read-only synthesis over local state) — the cost shape above.
2. **Laptop-local read-only monitors** — quota/pool reads, backup verification: the data is already on the laptop; a Muse cron pays subscription tokens to go read it remotely.
3. **Deterministic script checks as command payloads** with webhook delivery — no model tokens at all unless a check trips and escalates to an agentTurn.
4. **OpenClaw housekeeping** — already native; extend rather than rebuild.

Poor candidates: queue worker shifts and anything whose product is a GitHub write under Muse's review loop (see #2174 for the OpenCode side).

## Gates before scheduling fleet work here

1. Command Code 401 resolved or the agent primary repointed (config change rides the NixOS switch path).
2. Channel bindings or --no-deliver/webhook delivery chosen per job (heartbeat no-route skip is the symptom).
3. Token bridge: cron_run_receipts/task_runs joined to session usage and exported into Supabase, so the #2171 review (outcome/tokens/time vs OpenCode) covers scheduled runs too.
4. Inbound webhooks enabled if event-triggered OpenClaw jobs are wanted (ties to the repository_dispatch bridge in #2176).

## What #1728 + the switch do and do not do

Config today: ACP enabled with exactly one allowedAgent and one acpx agent (opencode). The merge + switch expands allowedAgents to [opencode, claude, codex, agy] with per-agent command overrides in both the embedded acpx config and ~/.acpx/config.json — that turns OpenClaw into a dispatcher that can hand coding work to ACP harnesses (and later the muse harness, #2012) instead of only running its own native turns. It does NOT fix the gateway-token env, hooks, channel bindings, or the Command Code 401.

## Acceptance

- Gates 1–3 closed; first two candidate classes running as OpenClaw scheduled jobs for a week, each run reviewed (outcome/tokens/time) against its Muse-cron baseline on #2171's comparison.

## Defect: OpenCode server handover is not in effect on the laptop — socket unit disabled, same-build switch darkened the port ~16s and cut the drain at 40ms

Drew's standing design: a server switch/restart passes the port and sessions over without dropping anything; a same-code switch needs no restart at all. Measured live during the 2026-11-16 agy 1.5.9 system switch (`nixos-rebuild switch`, SWITCH_EXIT=0, system generation 558 → 559):

### Evidence (all 2026-11-16, UTC)

- The opencode build did **not** change in this switch: `2.0.30+5b65c2a`, store path `bdkm7bd1gbx4i0cmk92zrzwc5x16ms00-opencode-2.0.30+5b65c2a` before and after. The service restarted anyway: pid 967757 → 3365330, new instance start 08:24:14Z.
- A 2-second-interval probe of `http://127.0.0.1:13420/api/config` across the switch recorded the port refused from **08:23:58Z through 08:24:12Z**, answering again at 08:24:14Z — ~16 seconds dark (479 healthy samples vs 8 refused in the run).
- Server log, old instance: `08:23:57.964Z draining running sessions and requests sessions=["ses_e5e1c9ad3c3ffeWx7ITHH5v49w","ses_e5e1c8eefd0ffehalIMX1R225d"] requests=0 grace=30000` — then 40ms later, `08:23:58.004Z shutdown ended with sessions or requests still running; interrupting them`. The announced 30s drain grace was not honored; something ended the drain almost immediately (the fork's drain ends early on a second termination signal — source of the second signal not yet identified).
- `opencode.socket`: `ActiveState=inactive`, `UnitFileState=disabled`; the 13420 listener is owned by the server process itself (`ss`: pid 3365330, fd 8). Socket activation is **not** in effect, which contradicts the 2026-11-11 follow-up on #8261 recording socket activation as adopted after the 2026-11-10 cascade. Either the adoption regressed or it never landed in the deployed unit set.

### Impact today: interruption, not loss

- Session store intact: `session_v2` held 22,937 ids before the switch; after: **0 lost**, 26 gained.
- Both interrupted sessions were re-warmed by the new instance (`scheduled session warming` 08:24:19Z) and produced successful route attempts from 08:24:20Z; the conductor's 08:25Z sweep lists both as progressing with 0 errors. No job permanently failed.
- But the guarantee Drew specified does not hold: the port went dark and in-flight turns were interrupted on a switch that changed nothing about the server.

### Fix asks

1. Enable `opencode.socket` so the port survives process swaps (or establish why the Nov 11 adoption did not stick and close that gap).
2. Find and remove the second-signal source that cuts the drain; the 30s grace must be honored.
3. Skip restarting the opencode service when the build/store path is unchanged across a switch.

Refs: #8261 (2026-11-10 cascade; adoption claim), #1822 (socket activation audit), #8255 (incumbent-defer cutover).

That is the key design question: the Zen door appears to read the *same plan meters* as the Go door for each workspace, so a naive registration of three new pools would render duplicate meters on the Space under a second id, while not registering them leaves the measured set incomplete.

Where registration is missing, verified against `origin/main` at `5b419f0c7b` (== local HEAD):

- `quota-extract.ts` `POOL_SPECS` contains only `opencode-go.drewrypope`, `opencode-go.popesdrew`, `opencode-go.developing-today-0` (lines ~576-598); no bare `opencode.*` ids, and `SHELL_POOLS` has no entry either.

Decide the attribution shape, then land it:

1. **Alias** the Zen rows onto the existing Go pools (`opencode.drewrypope` -> `opencode-go.drewrypope`, etc.) via `canonicalProviderId` / a service-id map in `quota-gather-map.ts`, so the measured set is complete without duplicating meters; or
2. **Register** three distinct Zen pools in `quota-extract.ts` if the Zen door is meant to hold independent meters (needs evidence that the identical values above are coincidental, not the same plan read).

## Acceptance

- Every providerId present in `quota-current.json providers[]` is either registered in `POOL_SPECS`/`SHELL_POOLS` or explicitly canonicalized/aliased, with `opencode.*` no longer unaccounted for.
- A test asserts the measured-provider census is covered by the registry (guards the #7835 defect class and this one).
- The Space renders the three Zen doors' meters, or deliberately renders them under their Go pools — no silent absence.

milestone.description: Pool & routing intelligence epic (#1334): lanes everywhere, live dispatch + babysitting, quota stewardship, reviewer oversight.

items.body:
## Work (Drew, 2026-10-27)

Stand up the babysitter as a live scheduled job (`openchamber-
babysitter`, every 20m), implementing #1185's design with #1192's
detector:

- Every round: enumerate ALL sessions at the laptop OpenChamber
  location (and any future locations), bound or unbound, and give
  each a verdict: progressing / stalled / done-unreported / blocked
  / walled (402-class) / idle.
- Stall rule (from #1192's census): suspect when ≥20 min since the
  session's last activity AND no live CI on its bound PR; confirm on
  a second suspect round or on expiry-equivalent silence. Nudge at
  most twice (message injection where the API shape is verified —
  verify by the session's next assistant message), then escalate to
  the fleet as a stuck-holder case.
- Report per round only what changed: new stalls, nudges sent,
  harvests ready (done-unreported sessions whose PR merged or work
  completed → the owning queue task gets completed by its lane, the
  babysitter flags it), quota snapshot per pool in use, and which
  pool each active session is drawing on + whether that choice looks
  effective (progress per the session's own checkpoints).
- Data out: append round observations to the babysitter log in the
  goal workspace (the pool-intelligence and meta-reviewer jobs read
  it); unbound sessions are observed, never driven.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] The job exists and has completed three rounds with per-session
      verdicts recorded.
- [ ] One real (or synthetic) stall is detected inside two rounds
      of the rule's threshold.
- [ ] Every report names each active session's pool; a session on a
      walled pool is flagged the round it happens.

Extends #1185; depends on openchamber#524 for the clean last-activity
field (rounds poll what's available until then). Child of the pool &
routing intelligence epic. Filed by Muse (operator) 2026-10-27.

# LANE 4 — MERGED-PR-AUDIT — AUDIT-7 tracking

Umbrella: https://github.com/developing-today/code/issues/13871

Scope: every PR merged since 2026-10-23 across:
- developing-today/code
- developing-today-forks/opencode
- developing-today-forks/openchamber

Method: one by one, read PR + diff in full; compare to spawning issue (especially Closes/fixes); check later PRs completed earlier gaps before filing; file real gaps/bugs/next-steps properly prioritised; apply documented outcome labels; per-PR ledger in final report.

Outcome labels (Lane 4 set, documented here and in final report):
- `audit:complete` — PR fully implemented its spawning issue / stated intent, no gap found
- `audit:partial` — PR partially implemented; gap filed (linked in ledger/comment)
- `audit:gap-filed` — a gap / unfiled next step was filed as a new issue from this PR
- `audit:bug-filed` — a bug found in the merged diff was filed as a new issue
- `audit:completed-later` — earlier gap was completed by a later merged PR (linked)
- `audit:no-issue` — PR had no spawning issue to compare against (verdict on stated intent only)

Progress will be posted at every slice boundary (per repo / per batch).

items.body:
## Problem

The queue's claim order is set entirely by fleet machinery — enqueue-time packet banding and the 2026-11-03 effectiveness re-tier — and none of it is Drew's order. Drew has never opened, edited, or connected to the queue store, and should never have to: his priorities exist as chat rulings and (since 2026-10-29) as the `expedite` / `next-up` issue labels, but nothing runs triage against them.

Worse, the one channel Drew did build is inverted. The 2026-10-29 label design maps `expedite` ⇒ priority 90 and `next-up` ⇒ priority 70, but the broker claims **lowest number first** (`ORDER BY priority ASC, created_at ASC`, fleet-queue `turso_queue.rs`; verified 2026-10-26, 2026-11-01, 2026-11-05, and again 2026-11-07). So the 15 issues Drew expedited on 2026-11-03 (the ID design tracks: #3447 + steps, #2898, #4000, #5047, #3789, #3792, #4837, and #3418) have their queue tasks sitting at priority 90 — the last band claimed — untouched since 2026-11-05. The inversion was flagged 2026-11-01 and never fixed; the label-honoring monitor duty was written against the old Supabase store and shows no action on the Turso store. The 2026-11-03 re-tier reused the same inverted reading (its "critical" band 70 claims after its "low" band 30).

Evidence snapshot (2026-11-07 ~19:20 CST): the next 20 tasks lanes will claim across the four pilot queues carry zero Drew-expressed priority; the plain-English top-of-queue is written up in `~/workspace/scratch/queue-top-plain-2026-11-07.md` (hatch-personal). A draft priorities brief — sourced entirely from Drew's goals and standing rulings — is at `~/workspace/scratch/drew-priorities-brief-draft-2026-11-07.md`, awaiting Drew's correction/ratification in chat.

## What to build

1. **Triage runs against the brief.** Once Drew ratifies the priorities brief, the hourly orchestration pass triages all four pilot queues against it: every band assignment or move cites the brief line that justifies it. Heuristic-only re-tiers (the 2026-11-03 pattern) are retired. Until ratification, no reprioritizing under this issue.
2. **Fix the label mapping.** `expedite` ⇒ ensure a live queue task and place it in the 10–20 band; `next-up` ⇒ ensure a task and place it in the 20–30 band (Drew's 2026-10-29 design, numbers flipped to the broker's real claim order). The honoring mechanism must run against the Turso fleet-queue store (the Supabase-era Duty 5 does not). The expedite/next-up set is Drew's: lanes never add or remove those labels on their own judgment.
3. **Plain-English top-of-queue, published on cadence.** The OpenCode & Muse Activity Space (or a successor view) shows the current top-of-queue in plain English — what each task is, which repo/issue, why it's at the top — refreshed on the orchestration pass cadence from the live store. Drew reads the order there; he never opens the queue table.
4. **Chat rulings become queue order in the same pass.** Any Drew ruling of the form "X matters" / "do X first" / "prioritize #N" is translated by the orchestrator into the labels + queue priority above in the same pass it is given, and time-boxed rulings record their window and expire on schedule.

## Acceptance

- [ ] Brief ratified by Drew (corrected version filed where the orchestration pass reads it).
- [ ] Label mapping flipped and verified by readback: an expedited issue's task reads in the 10–20 band in the Turso store; the current 15-issue expedite set is re-banded accordingly.
- [ ] One orchestration pass completes citing brief lines for its triage moves.
- [ ] The Activity Space (or successor) shows a plain-English top-of-queue stamped with its read time, refreshed by the pass.
- [ ] A Drew chat priority ruling given after ratification is reflected in labels + band within one orchestration pass, with no Drew clicks.

Refs: Drew's ruling 2026-11-07 19:12 CST (the queue's order is not his; make the system useful). Related: #7016 (standing issue↔queue reconciliation), #6853 (lane registry), #6423 (packet validation).

  which login each read reflects.
- Pool coverage table: for each pool in the provider-quota registry
  (DeepSeek routes, OpenAI, Meta High Usage, Claude routes,
  Antigravity), the quota source, its freshness in practice, and
  whether `~/tools/provider-usage/check-usage.py` +

- Burn measurement: for one finished session, reconstruct its pool
  burn from available records; state the error bars honestly.

      per-session attribution method or gap).
- [ ] One real session's pool + burn is reconstructed end-to-end, or

items.body:
## Problem (found by pilot #1188, 2026-10-26)

Two routing systems now coexist and nobody has reconciled them:

- **The fleet's policy** (Drew, 2026-10-26 + the POOL MAP in the
  provider-quota registry): Workhorse-first (DeepSeek Flash high,
  Luna Max, Sonnet), Frontier only on evidence or for design, Fast
  for mechanical work; measurement gate (quota read ≤60 min old,
  ≥85% of window = no new heavy work); plan quotas only, never PAYG;
  OpenAI the final reserve; Astra gated; Antigravity Argon watched.
- **OpenChamber's own classifier** (`~/.config/openchamber/routing.json`
  on the laptop): categories trivial / research / implement / hard,
  bound today to — trivial → antigravity gemini-3.8-flash (high),
  research → opencode-go gpt-6-luna (max), implement → opencode-go
  muse-spark-1.3-contributor (high), fallback → claude-code
  claude-haiku-5-5.

The bindings may or may not match the policy — nobody has checked
them side by side (e.g. trivial work defaults to the Antigravity tier
the pool map says to watch; the implement default's pool isn't in the
quota-attribution picture yet). The dispatcher (#1187) will route by
one of these; it must not be by accident.

## Work

- Produce the mapping table: fleet tier (Fast/Workhorse/Frontier) ×
  OpenChamber category, with the pool each binding draws on and its
  quota source.
- Flag every binding that conflicts with the POOL MAP gates (watched
  tiers as defaults, ungated Astra-class routes, pools with no quota
  read) and propose the corrected binding.
- Recommend which system is canonical at dispatch time (fleet policy
  expressed through OpenChamber categories is the expected answer —
  confirm or refute with reasons).

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] Mapping table + conflict list exist in the goal workspace and
      are linked from epic #1234.
- [ ] Each conflict has a proposed corrected binding, or an explicit
      "keep, because" with the reason recorded.
- [ ] Pilot #1191's trial runs use the mapped categories so its
      evidence lands on the real configuration.

Child of epic #1234. Filed by Muse (operator) 2026-10-26.
